analysis.one_liner: Britannia Industries makes and sells packaged biscuits, bread, cakes, rusk and dairy products across India and a growing set of export markets, under brands like Good Day, Tiger, Marie Gold and NutriChoice.
analysis.whats_happening: Britannia reported Q2 FY27 (September quarter) results on 2026-11-05: revenue from operations of roughly ₹5,542 crore, up 16.6% year-on-year, with volume growth of 13%. Net profit rose about 10% YoY (sources cite figures between ₹705 crore and ₹726 crore - likely a standalone vs consolidated difference, not fully verified). The stock fell sharply the next trading day (-3.4% on 2026-11-06) as gross margin contracted 203 basis points to 39.6% on input-cost inflation, overshadowing the strong volume number.
analysis.plain_terms: Britannia is selling more biscuits and bakery products than a year ago - volumes grew 13%, which is a genuinely healthy demand signal, not just price increases. But the cost of wheat flour, palm oil, milk and packaging laminate has risen faster than the price hikes the company has been able to pass on, so profit margins are getting squeezed even as sales grow. The stock has fallen about 24% from its October 2024 peak, reflecting the market reassessing how much it should pay for a very expensive stock whose margins have stopped expanding. This isn't a crash caused by any corporate action - there's been no recent demerger or split - it's a genuine valuation correction.
analysis.quarters: Q2 FY27 revenue grew 16.6% YoY to about ₹5,542 crore on 13% volume growth, but EBITDA grew only about 6% as gross margin fell 203 bps YoY to 39.6% - wheat flour was up 9% QoQ, refined palm oil up 11% QoQ/17% YoY, milk up 16% YoY, and laminate up 7% QoQ/18% YoY. H1 FY27 revenue crossed ₹10,000 crore for the first time (cited as ₹10,506-10,598 crore depending on source, up 12-13% YoY), with H1 net profit around ₹1,312 crore, up 12% YoY. Management flagged that a GST rate cut on biscuits to 5%, effective 2026-09-22, disrupted ₹5/₹10 price-point packaging across roughly 85% of the business - this adds short-term noise to period comparisons and management said the 3.5% price hike taken so far covers only part of the cost inflation, with milk prices not showing their usual seasonal softening.
analysis.performance_read: The stock is down 20.75% over the last year versus the Nifty's -2.3% and peer Nestlé's +1.87% - a sharp, broad underperformance. Over 3 years it has returned just 7.23% against the Nifty's 28.83%, a large and sustained lag. Over 5 years it is roughly in line with both the Nifty (38.83% vs 38.29%) and Nestlé (40.5%), so the underperformance is concentrated in the last one-to-three years. The stock is 23.6% below its October 2024 peak of ₹6,258.44, now sitting between its 52-week low of ₹4,537.9 and high of ₹6,083.68. There has been no recent split or demerger (last split was a 2:1 in November 2018), so this drawdown is a genuine price correction, not a corporate-action artifact.
analysis.valuation_read: The stock trades around 45-46x trailing earnings (various sources show a range from roughly 44.5x to 62.5x depending on date and EPS base used), well above the broader market multiple. It is expensive largely because of its track record of very high capital efficiency (ROE ~55%) and FMCG brand moat, which the market has historically paid up for. Whether that premium is still warranted is the open question: EBITDA grew only 6% against 16.6% revenue growth this quarter, so the stock is priced for a margin recovery that hasn't yet shown up consistently in the numbers.
analysis.growth_read: Growth this quarter was genuinely volume-led - 13% YoY volume growth alongside revenue growth of 16.6% is a healthier mix than pure price-led growth, especially in a commodity-exposed business. But the volume strength isn't yet converting proportionally into profit growth: EBITDA rose only about 6% as margins compressed, so top-line growth is currently outrunning bottom-line growth.
analysis.health_read: Profitability-to-cash conversion looks sound on the metrics available: ROE of roughly 55% and ROCE of roughly 56%, with a Debt-to-Equity ratio of about 0.29 and modest debt (~₹1,346 crore) against a large profit base. This is a low financial-risk business. The risk here is on the business/operating side - input cost inflation (wheat, palm oil, milk, packaging) squeezing margins - not balance-sheet stress.
analysis.ownership_read: Promoters (Wadia group entities) hold 50.55% as of September 2026, a stable figure with zero pledging reported - a clean signal on promoter financial stress. LIC has been reported increasing its stake to around 5%, and combined institutional holding (FII + DII) is substantial. One governance watchpoint worth flagging: Britannia's FY26 secretarial compliance filing disclosed ongoing litigation involving promoter directors before the Supreme Court tied to Bombay Dyeing and SEBI Act matters, and there has been publicly reported discord within the Wadia family (including Jehangir Wadia's past exit from Wadia Group company boards) - this is a background governance factor, not a current financial red flag.
strengths: 13% YoY volume growth in Q2 FY27 - demand-led, not just price hikes
ROE of roughly 55% and ROCE of roughly 56% on a Debt-to-Equity ratio of only about 0.29 - highly capital-efficient with low leverage
Zero promoter pledge on a stable 50.55% promoter stake
H1 FY27 revenue crossed ₹10,000 crore for the first time, up 12-13% YoY
watchpoints: Gross margin fell 203 bps YoY to 39.6% in Q2 FY27 as wheat, palm oil, milk and laminate costs rose in double digits
EBITDA grew only ~6% against 16.6% revenue growth - profit growth is lagging sales growth
Stock down 20.75% over 1 year and just 7.23% over 3 years versus the Nifty's 28.83% - a sustained valuation de-rating from the October 2024 peak
GST rate-cut transition (biscuits to 5% GST from 2026-09-22) disrupted ₹5/₹10 pack pricing across ~85% of the business, adding short-term noise to period comparisons
Promoter-director litigation before the Supreme Court tied to Bombay Dyeing/SEBI Act matters, disclosed in the FY26 compliance filing - a governance item to track, not a resolved matter
analysis.one_thing: Whether Britannia can push through further price increases to rebuild gross margin back toward prior-year levels without losing the 13% volume momentum it just posted - the Q3 FY27 (December quarter) results, expected around early February 2027 (not verified), will show whether margin recovery is underway or input-cost inflation keeps outpacing pricing.
analysis.data_notes: Cross-checked across multiple sources: revenue growth (~16.6% YoY) and 13% volume growth are consistent across several reports; gross margin contraction (-203 bps to 39.6%) and input-cost commentary (wheat, palm oil, milk, laminate) are consistent; ROE (~55%), ROCE (~56%) and Debt/Equity (~0.29) are consistent; promoter stake (50.55%) and zero pledge are consistent. Net profit for Q2 FY27 varies across sources (₹705.5 crore to ₹726 crore) - likely a standalone-vs-consolidated discrepancy, not independently verified to the rupee. Shareholding sub-category splits (DII reported as both ~5.13% and ~21.47% in different sources) were inconsistent - the fuller breakdown summing closer to 100% was used. P/E multiple also varies by source and date (44.5x-62.5x cited); used the most commonly cited ~46x figure near the results date, not recomputed against the verified last close.
